findings.trigger: The comment at lines 102-108 (in encrypt_token) documents that TokenEncryptionError descends from ConfigServiceError, that none of the previously-caught tuples caught it, and that the fix was to add an explicit `except ConfigServiceError`. That fix was applied only to encrypt_token (line 102). get_token_security_status (26-75), get_migration_help (130-167) and get_security_audit (170-207) still only catch (ImportError, AttributeError, RuntimeError) and (ValueError, TypeError, KeyError) - not ConfigServiceError. If service.get_token_security_status() / service.get_migration_help() / service.get_security_audit() can also raise a ConfigServiceError or a subclass (plausible, since it's the shared error base for this service and its token/config handling), pressing 'check token status', 'migration help' or 'run security audit' hits the exact bug just fixed on the sibling route: an unhandled exception and Flask's generic blank 500 page instead of the route's own JSON error body.
findings.suggestion: Add the same `except ConfigServiceError as e: ... return jsonify({...}), 500` branch (before the ImportError/AttributeError/RuntimeError branch) to get_token_security_status, get_migration_help and get_security_audit, mirroring the fix already in encrypt_token.
findings.unsure_why: services/web/security_service.py is not in this section's source, so I cannot confirm whether get_token_security_status/get_migration_help/get_security_audit actually raise ConfigServiceError (or a subclass) in any real code path the way TokenEncryptionError does for encrypt_token. The parallel is strong (same service, same route pattern, one sibling demonstrably needed this exact fix) but unverified for the other three.

findings.trigger: get_cached_servers() (272-283) branches on _config_cache.is_valid(). While the cache is fresh (within max_cache_age, 15 minutes per line 240), it returns ConfigCache.get_servers() (124), which is whatever set_config() stored - and set_config() (31-47) always runs the config through _optimize_config_for_memory(), which keeps only 'name', 'docker_name', 'allowed_actions' and 'info' per server and drops every other field, including 'display_name' and 'order'. Once the cache is stale or was cleared, the same function instead returns get_cached_config().get('servers', []) (261-271), which goes through get_config_service().get_config() and is the full, untrimmed server list. A caller of get_cached_servers() that reads e.g. display_name or order therefore gets the real value or a silent default (docker_name, or order 999) depending only on how many minutes have passed since the cache was last (re)populated - the same call can answer differently for the same underlying config, and nothing signals which shape it just received.
findings.suggestion: Make get_cached_servers() return a consistent shape regardless of cache freshness - either always trim to the same fields, or have the 'cache valid' branch return the same full server list the 'cache invalid' branch does (and keep the trimmed version only behind the class's own get_servers() for its documented autocomplete use).
findings.unsure_why: This section does not include the callers of get_cached_servers(). Both docstrings say it's 'optimized for autocomplete', so if every real caller only ever reads name/docker_name/allowed_actions, the shape difference never produces a visibly wrong value. I can't see enough of the codebase to confirm whether any caller relies on display_name/order from this specific function.

notes: Two smaller things noticed but not raised as findings because I could not state a concrete trigger for either: (1) utils/config_cache.py _optimize_config_for_memory's essential_server['info'] = server.get('info', {defaults}) only supplies the default dict when the 'info' key is absent - a server whose config explicitly has "info": null would cache info=None, and any downstream code doing info.get(...) on a cached server would then fail; I don't have visibility into who reads this field to say whether that ever happens. (2) cogs/ddc_ui.py PrivateView.__init_subclass__ overrides self.timeout to AUTO_CLOSE_SECONDS (60) whenever the close button would be alone on its row; this is fine for every current subclass (all are ephemeral, none sets timeout=None), but a future PrivateView subclass that deliberately wants persistence (timeout=None) with a lone close button would have that silently overridden - not a bug in the code as it stands today, just a trap for later. Both are recorded here per the instructions rather than as findings, since neither has a concrete trigger in the code actually shown to me.
